q: How much of the paper's headline 'low genome similarity' (mean MASH d=0.94 in our re-run) is an artefact of accession-collection strategy? Our 231-genome matrix shows a small cluster of near-identical pairs (~1.1% at d<0.05). Are these independent isolates of the same species deposited under different accessions, and would a species-deduplicated matrix change the 92.7%-unrelated headline?
basis: In our re-replication: 592 of 53,130 MASH pairs (1.11%) have d<0.05 despite being different accessions, hinting at redundancy in the paper's 236-genome collection strategy that inflates 'diversity' claims.
next_steps: Cluster the 231 genomes at MASH d<0.05 to produce a species-level dereplicated set (target: skani or MASH+greedy 95% ANI). Recompute pairwise similarity and the singleton-protein-cluster fraction on the dereplicated set. If the 92.7% pairs-unrelated headline is stable (say 90%+ still), the diversity claim is robust; if it drops below ~75% the paper is significantly oversampling near-duplicates. Compare the collection date distribution (accession prefixes) to see whether 2020-2022 pandemic-era deposits are the redundant ones.

q: Does the paper's PHASTER-based prophage set (36 prophages ≥20 kb from 10 host genomes) systematically miss fully-integrated ancient prophages lacking canonical phage structural genes, biasing the 'clear prophage↔lytic genome boundary' claim?
basis: PHASTER's classification (intact/questionable/incomplete) is length- and marker-gene-driven. The paper's ≥20 kb filter almost certainly discards heavily-decayed ancient prophages that only contain regulator + integrase remnants. Our replication did not re-run this step (PHASTER is a web service).
next_steps: Install VirSorter2 v2.2 + geNomad v1.7 in a conda env on uicgpu; run both on the 10 Bacillus host genomes named in Table S3; compare the union of predicted prophage regions to the paper's 36 PHASTER-only set. Score how many ancient/decayed prophages are recovered by VirSorter2 but missed by PHASTER, then re-derive the prophage-vs-lytic MASH boundary and see if the visual 'clear boundary' persists.

q: Are singleton protein clusters (49% of 6,875 clusters in our re-run) enriched in the smaller Bacillus phage genomes (<50 kb), meaning the paper's 'large unknown-function fraction' is actually a small-phage hypothetical-protein bias rather than genuine novel-function diversity across all size classes?
basis: Our MMseqs2 clustering at 30% identity produced 3,351 singleton clusters. Small phages (~<50 kb, 88/231 in our set = 38%) are known to be dominated by hypothetical proteins with few homologs. If singletons cluster in this size bin, the 'unknown gene fragment' story is partly explained by well-known small-phage annotation drift, not novel biology.
next_steps: Tag each of the 6,875 clusters with the length distribution of the source genomes it appears in. Compute Spearman correlation between mean-source-genome-length and cluster-size. If small-genome clusters are enriched in singletons (rho < -0.3), the interpretation of 'unknown functions' shifts to 'small-phage annotation deficit'. Also cross-search the singleton reps against Pfam35 + eggNOG-mapper to quantify the true novel-family fraction.

q: The paper's 'two lysis-module types' (Type I / Type II, from Tables S6/S7 based on 3 focal phages) is claimed to gate cross-species Bacillus infestation, but only 25 vs 105 sequences are listed. What is the actual frequency of each type across the full 231-lytic panel, and does the type distribution correlate quantitatively with host range?
basis: Our replication captured all 231 lytic genomes but did not annotate the lysis module. A hidden Markov / HMMsearch scan of each type against the 231-panel proteomes would put an unambiguous number on the type distribution.
next_steps: Build a two-model HMM library from the Type-I and Type-II lysis-module protein alignments (aligned via MAFFT, model built via HMMER v3.4 hmmbuild). Run hmmsearch against the 35,069-protein 231-panel proteome. Count Type-I vs Type-II hits per genome. Correlate hit-type with host species (extracted from GenBank source qualifiers) via chi-square. If the association is significant (p < 0.01), the paper's cross-species-infestation claim is quantitatively supported; if not, it is over-generalised from n=3 focal phages.

q: How stable is the 20-focal-phage tree topology across independent methods (paper's Mauve/Easyfig visual clustering vs our MASH BIONJ vs a proteome-based tree)? A normalized Robinson-Foulds distance would separate genuine evolutionary signal from single-method artefacts.
basis: Our MASH BIONJ tree of the 20 focal phages (mash20_nj.nwk) recovers clear Wbetavirus and SPP1-like clades that match the Table S4 lineage assignments, but 91% of MASH pairs are at d ≈ 1.0 so much of the tree topology is essentially arbitrary (long branches with weak support). A proteome-based tree from shared MMseqs2 clusters would be an independent check.
next_steps: Extract the 460 protein clusters shared by ≥2 of the 20 focal phages. Encode each phage as a binary presence/absence vector over these 460 clusters. Build a UPGMA / NJ tree on Jaccard distances. Compute normalized RF distance to (a) our MASH BIONJ tree and (b) the ICTV lineage assignments in Table S4. If RF < 0.3 across methods, the 20-phage clade structure is real; if RF > 0.6 it is method-driven and the paper's Fig 5/6 clade-based conclusions need caveating. Also run IQ-TREE on the largest 5 shared-cluster protein alignments concatenated to get bootstrap support.
